headings.title: Definition and Classification of Postpartum Haemorrhage
headings.content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) remains a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality globally, with a particularly high burden in low- and middle-income countries like Nigeria. Traditionally, PPH is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours following a vaginal birth, or 1000 mL or more following a caesarean section. However, clinical definitions also encompass any amount of bleeding that compromises maternal hemodynamic stability. PPH is further classified into two distinct categories: primary (early) PPH and secondary (late) PPH. Primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours after delivery and is most frequently caused by uterine atony. Secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours up to 12 weeks postpartum, commonly resulting from retained products of conception, subinvolution of the placental site, or genital tract infection. Understanding these definitions and classifications is crucial for nursing students, as prompt identification dictates the urgency and appropriateness of the clinical response. In Nigerian healthcare settings, where resources can sometimes be constrained, recognizing the threshold for PPH ensures that midwives and nurses initiate life-saving interventions before the parturient spirals into hypovolemic shock. Accurate estimation of blood loss is vital, as visual estimation often leads to significant underestimation of actual blood volume lost, delaying critical treatment protocols.

headings.title: Physiological Changes and the 4 Ts of Postpartum Haemorrhage
headings.content: During pregnancy, a woman experiences significant physiological adaptations, notably a 30 to 50 percent expansion in blood volume to meet the metabolic demands of the gravid uterus and fetus. This hypervolemia allows a parturient to tolerate substantial blood loss during delivery without immediately showing classic signs of shock, which can dangerously delay recognition. To systematically organize the underlying causes of PPH, clinical educators utilize the mnemonic known as the '4 Ts': Tone, Tissue, Trauma, and Thrombin. 'Tone' refers to uterine atony, which accounts for approximately 70 to 80 percent of all PPH cases due to the failure of the myometrium to contract and compress blood vessels at the placental site. 'Tissue' involves the retention of placental fragments, membranes, or blood clots that prevent effective uterine contraction. 'Trauma' encompasses lacerations of the cervix, vagina, or perineum, as well as uterine rupture or inversion resulting from operative deliveries or rapid labor. Finally, 'Thrombin' represents coagulation disorders, either pre-existing or acquired during pregnancy, such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), severe preeclampsia, or amniotic fluid embolism. For nursing students, mastering the 4 Ts provides a structured mental framework to rapidly evaluate, triage, and manage any bleeding emergency in the maternity ward.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: Identifying the etiology and risk factors associated with postpartum haemorrhage is an essential competency for maternal-neonatal nurses. While PPH can occur unexpectedly in women with no apparent risk factors, certain conditions significantly heighten the likelihood of excessive bleeding. Major risk factors related to uterine atony include grand multiparity, overdistension of the uterus (such as in multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, or macrosomia), prolonged labor, rapid labor, and chorioamnionitis or intrapartum fever. Factors linked to tissue complications include retained placenta, morbidly adherent placenta (placenta accreta spectrum), and a history of previous uterine surgery or curettage. Traumatic causes are frequently associated with instrumental deliveries (forceps or vacuum extractions), episiotomies, precipitous delivery, and nulliparity with large babies. Coagulation-related risks involve pre-existing bleeding disorders like von Willebrand disease, anticoagulant therapy, severe pregnancy-induced hypertension, and abruptio placentae. In Nigeria, home births attended by unskilled birth attendants or delayed presentation to a health facility due to transportation challenges often exacerbate these risks, turning manageable etiologies into life-threatening emergencies. Thorough antenatal booking history and continuous intrapartum risk assessment allow nurses to anticipate PPH and prepare emergency supplies proactively.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Early Recognition
headings.content: Clinical assessment and early recognition of PPH are vital to preventing maternal mortality. Nurses must maintain high vigilance during the immediate postpartum period, routinely assessing vital signs, uterine consistency, and the quantity of lochia. The uterus should be palpated frequently to ensure it remains well-contracted, firm, and centrally located; a boggy, soft uterus indicates atony. Quantitative or gravimetric measurement of blood loss—such as weighing surgical pads and collecting blood in calibrated drapes—provides a much more objective assessment than visual estimation alone, which notoriously underestimates blood loss. Nurses must also watch for subtle early signs of hypovolemic shock, including maternal restlessness, tachycardia, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill, even before a measurable drop in blood pressure occurs. In Nigerian clinical practice, where patient-to-nurse ratios can be high, implementing structured postpartum observation charts and empowering lower-cadre staff or relatives to report heavy bleeding immediately can drastically improve outcomes. Early recognition allows the multidisciplinary team to transition swiftly from routine postpartum care to active resuscitation and emergency management protocols.

headings.title: Prevention and Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour
headings.content: Prevention and active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) represent the single most effective intervention to reduce the incidence of postpartum haemorrhage. AMTSL is a proactive package of care administered immediately following the birth of the baby to facilitate placental delivery and prevent uterine atony. It consists of three core components: first, the administration of a uterotonic drug (preferably oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly or intravenously) within one minute of delivery; second, controlled cord traction (CCT) combined with counter-pressure on the gravid uterus (brandane maneuver); and third, massage of the uterine fundus immediately after the placenta is delivered and every 15 minutes for the first two hours. Oxytocin is the uterotonic agent of choice because it has rapid onset, high efficacy, and minimal side effects. In environments where oxytocin storage is compromised by erratic electricity or lack of refrigeration, alternatives such as sublingual misoprostol or injectable ergometrine are utilized, keeping contraindications like hypertension in mind. For nursing and midwifery students in Nigeria, mastering AMTSL is mandatory, as its routine implementation in primary health centres and tertiary hospitals has proven to save countless lives by preventing excessive blood loss before it begins.

headings.title: Emergency Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: When PPH occurs despite preventative measures, immediate emergency medical and surgical management must be deployed in a structured, stepwise manner. The emergency response starts with calling for help, mobilizing the multidisciplinary team, and initiating basic resuscitation (ABCDE approach). Bimanual uterine compression and aortic compression are immediate physical measures to temporarily reduce bleeding while uterotonics are prepared. Medical management involves administering additional uterotonics sequentially, such as high-dose oxytocin infusions, ergometrine, carboprost (prostaglandin F2-alpha), and sublingual or rectal misoprostol. If medical management fails to control uterine atony, surgical interventions must be escalated rapidly. These include uterine massage, insertion of an intrauterine balloon tamponade (such as the Bakri balloon or simplified condom catheter tamponade), compression sutures (like the B-Lynch suture), uterine or internal iliac artery ligation, and ultimately, as a last resort to save the mother's life, a subtotal or total hysterectomy. In resource-limited Nigerian settings, condom-catheter hydrostatic balloon tamponade has proven to be an affordable, life-saving alternative to commercial balloons. Nurses play a critical role in preparing surgical trays, assisting with procedures, monitoring fluid balance, and communicating effectively with the surgical and anesthetic teams.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Resuscitation Protocols in Nigerian Clinical Practice
headings.content: Effective nursing care and resuscitation protocols during a PPH emergency require precise teamwork, clear communication, and adherence to evidence-based guidelines. Upon recognizing severe PPH, the nurse must immediately activate the hospital's emergency response team, ensure large-bore intravenous access (16G or 18G) in both arms, and draw blood for baseline investigations including full blood count, blood typing, cross-matching, and coagulation profile. Fluid resuscitation should be initiated with warmed crystalloids (Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate), while preparing for emergency blood transfusion. In many Nigerian tertiary centers, accessing safe blood can be challenging due to donor shortages or processing delays; therefore, utilizing hospital-based family replacement donors or emergency group-O negative/type-specific blood is critical. Nurses must institute continuous monitoring of vital signs, oxygen saturation, and urine output via an indwelling catheter with a urometer to assess renal perfusion and prevent acute kidney injury. Accurate documentation of all interventions, fluid intake, and estimated blood loss is vital for clinical handover and legal records. Providing psychological support and reassurance to the terrified mother and her family members is also an indispensable duty of the compassionate nurse throughout the resuscitation process.

headings.title: Complications and Long-Term Prognosis
headings.content: The complications and long-term prognosis of postpartum haemorrhage depend heavily on the speed and efficacy of the initial intervention. Acute complications of severe PPH include profound hypovolemic shock, dilutional coagulopathy, acute kidney injury (AKI) resulting from renal tubular necrosis, and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS). Women who experience massive blood loss may also suffer from Sheehan's syndrome, an ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary gland caused by severe hypotension, which leads to postpartum hypopituitarism (manifesting as failure to lactate, amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency). Psychologically, survivors of near-miss PPH and traumatic deliveries are at a significantly heightened risk of postpartum depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). In resource-constrained settings in Nigeria, long-term physical morbidity can also include chronic pelvic pain, secondary infertility resulting from emergency hysterectomy or Asherman's syndrome, and the social stigma associated with prolonged maternal illness. Student nurses must recognize that clinical recovery extends far beyond hospital discharge; comprehensive follow-up care must include nutritional support for anaemia, mental health screening, family planning counseling, and scheduled postnatal check-ups to ensure holistic maternal rehabilitation.
